title: Coontec’s AEZIZ v3.0 Wins GS Certification, Targets Public Sector - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
content: Coontec said on Nov. 9 that its software and artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain security platform, AEZIZ v3.0, has received Grade 1 Good Software (GS) certification from Korea Testing Certification (KTC). The company plans to strengthen its supply chain security business targeting public institutions and financial companies. The AEZIZ v3.0 feature that met the Grade 1 GS certification requirements is software composition analysis (SCA). SCA identifies and analyzes open-source components, licenses and security vulnerabilities in software. In addition to SCA, AEZIZ offers supply chain management (SCM), open-source intake management (RMS) and AI component analysis (AICA). The platform can analyze binary files as well as source code. Binary files are program files converted from source code into a format that computers can execute. This allows the platform to analyze third-party commercial software even when source code is difficult to obtain. GS certification is a national certification program that evaluates software quality. It assesses functional suitability, performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security and maintainability. Grade 1-certified products qualify for preferential procurement of commercial software by public institutions. Coontec uses data on more than 8.6 million software components and over 400,000 vulnerabilities in its analysis. The platform also generates software bills of materials (SBOMs), which list software components, in international standard formats. It can also generate AI bills of materials (AI-BOMs) showing library dependencies within AI models. “To identify threats before attackers do, we must first understand what is inside a system,” said Bang Hyuk-joon, chief executive officer of Coontec. “We will continue enhancing AEZIZ so that public-sector and financial customers can identify risks in software components and AI models before deployment and respond as quickly as possible.”

title: Last Orders in the Alps: Riding a BMW R 1300 GS through the Dolomites - Autocar India
content: Somewhere on the approach to Passo Falzarego, I kept the throttle open well beyond the sensible braking point, then feathered the brakes far too late and tipped the fully loaded 250kg BMW R 1300 GS into a corner. The horizon tilted at what felt like 49 degrees. The motorcycle took it all in its stride. The suspension swallowed the bend; when I rolled back onto the throttle, the Akrapovič exhaust cleared its throat, the traction control moderated the conversation between the drive shaft and the rear wheel, and the front wheel lifted in a little wheelie of triumph. I carried on to the next hairpin with a smile plastered across my face, as it had been so many times that week. Around me, the Dolomites were having the best week of their year, in the middle of October. The larches had turned gold and rust, the pale rock towers stood bathed in sunshine, and the tarmac was dry and, for long stretches, entirely ours. Every so often another rider came the other way, two fingers held out in the wordless handshake motorcyclists everywhere seem to have agreed on. And there, around the next hairpin, a thought arrived, uninvited and slightly absurd: all of this had begun with an innocent phone call from Abhijit, my brother-in-law. Abhijit was twiddling thumbs between jobs, with time on his hands and a recently purchased Ducati Multistrada V4S standing in his parking bay. He called me for advice on where to take it for a road trip. The conversation wandered from Goa to Rajasthan, and to Kerala, but none of that caught his fancy. Then he said, “What about riding to Ladakh?” I told him that riding in Ladakh is wonderful, but getting there from Mumbai is tiresome. “It’s not like Europe,” I said rather offhandedly, “where riding from Munich to the Alps is almost as enjoyable as riding in them.” That was the tipping point. The Alps stuck to the conversation like a rash, and the mere mention of them infused my voice with a whole new level of excitement and elation. By the end of the call, what had started as Abhijit’s search for a week-long ride had turned into a plot in which I had committed to planning a 12-day loop out of Munich through Germany, Switzerland, Italy and Austria, with me becoming a party to the plan. Those eight minutes on the phone ultimately ended up costing me Rs 2.5 lakh – money very well spent! Then I started looking for a motorcycle. My first instinct was to find something in the 600cc to 800cc category. But my former Autocar India colleague, Ouseph Chacko, now a BMW-certified GS instructor, and Rishaad Mody, this magazine’s motorcycle editor, were unanimous in their advice: “Take the BMW R 1300 GS. It’s a sweet, sweet motorcycle.” That was all the convincing I needed. I asked BMW for one, and they said yes. Abhijit also chose the GS and rented one for the trip. To plan our ride, I hopped, skipped and jumped between Google Maps, Auntie Claude and Booking.com, checking distances, looking for route advice and good food, and finding mostly affordable two-bedroom apartments with free cancellation as close to the day of stay as possible. Now, on a bend near Passo Falzarego, with the larches blazing, the great limestone walls of the Dolomites bathed in warm, slanting sunlight, and the road empty beneath a motorcycle that was mine for twelve days, I smiled wistfully at the phone call that had started it all. Nine days earlier, I had stepped off an Etihad flight in Munich after an intentional 24-hour break in Abu Dhabi, so I met the GS without a trace of jet lag. The comfortable cabin, attentive service and warm hospitality onboard meant I swung a leg over the saddle well rested and energetic. We left Munich and rode south, deeper into Bavaria, the Alps growing larger in my visor until Wallgau, a village of timbered balconies and painted house fronts, appeared at their foot. For dinner that evening at the Gasthof Zur Post, I did what any traveller in Bavaria is duty-bound to do and ordered the pork knuckle. It arrived beneath a cap of crackling the size of a small cushion and left as bare bones. The next day, Austria’s Fernpass and Reschenpass unspooled in long, flowing curves, easy miles in which to settle into the GS before the real work began. Then we dropped into the Italian part of Tyrol and spent two nights in Laces, in the Vinschgau Valley, among apple orchards so laden that the branches were propped up on crutches. This also meant delicious apple strudel at most places we ate at. Carrying on, we crossed into Switzerland, over the Ofenpass and through the Swiss National Park, on a road lined with pine forest and almost no traffic, before dropping down to Poschiavo, with the Bernina Pass on its doorstep. I had set the mode button to toggle between Dynamic for the long, easy stretches, Dynamic Pro for the passes, and Rain for wet-weather days. By then, my thumb knew which one to reach for before my head did. Crossing back into Italy, we spent a night near Bormio, and the next morning we came face to face with the mighty Passo Stelvio sitting at 2,757 metres (9,045 feet). We rode the famed 48 hairpins of the north face. At the Tibet Hütte, the café at the summit, I ate apple strudel with fresh cream and watched cyclists grind up the last bends under their own power, grunting at the effort. I prayed to the Almighty to cure them of this affliction that makes them torture themselves and took another bite of my delicious dessert. At the bottom of the Stelvio, we turned east through the Vinschgau, past Merano and Bolzano, and powered on to Villandro and the Dolomites. Rumpelehof stands in the hamlet of Stofls, on the outskirts of Villandro. It is a working farm with self-catering apartments, where Alexandra and Raimund Gasser raise cattle and sheep. Mornings began with bleats and bull bellows rather than an alarm. Our two-bedroom apartment looked straight across at the Dolomites, a spectacular view, especially at sunrise. There were apple trees on the farm, and Raimund told me I could eat the apples without washing them because no pesticide had been sprayed on them. The only thing to watch for was worms. They were delicious, the apples, not the worms. For dinner on both evenings, we rode down to Gasthof Pizzeria Rustica in Villandro, a sprawling, warmly lit place that unfolds room after room, each one fuller and louder than the last. We came across two lads from Punjab working in its kitchen and had a hearty conversation with them. It was hunting season, so game crowded the menu. One night I ate a pizza with local salami and fiery peppers, the heat sneaking up like a rumour. The next, I had tagliatelle with a deer ragù – rich, slow-cooked, laced with pepper and finished with Parmigiano Reggiano – that I would happily have crossed a mountain pass for. Fortunately, I only had to ride down a hill. On our first day there, we rode a loop from the farm through Ponte Gardena, Ortisei and Selva, then up Passo Sella to Canazei, over the Pordoi and back the same way. The Alps had been wonderful, but it was the Dolomites that took my heart, perhaps because we arrived just as the autumn colours peaked. Near Canazei, through my helmet, I heard a familiar thump. My heart told me what it was before I turned my head. Sure enough, a Royal Enfield was chugging up towards Passo Pordoi. I excitedly flagged it down. The rider, from Lake Garda, said he loved everything about India and Royal Enfield. Around us were Multistradas, GSs and Africa Twins, while this humble Bullet chugged up the slope, holding its own, its rider in no hurry at all. The two engines could hardly have been more different. His Bullet, a single cylinder that thumps. Mine, a boxer, with two cylinders poking out either side like elbows at a crowded table, a layout BMW has been refining since 1923. Blip the throttle at a standstill and the GS rocks sideways, like a large dog shifting its weight. Both are unmistakable, and both certainly have character. It was the kind of day that leaves you a little melancholic and nostalgic, quietly happy at the way things have turned out. So, the next morning, when I leaned the GS into the hairpin on the road to Falzarego that opened this story, my mind went back to Abhijit’s phone call and how a casual conversation about Ladakh had brought me here. Mornings at that altitude start with a nip in the air, which is where the GS earns some of its keep. Thumb the heated grips and seat into life, and within two minutes you are sitting on a warm bench with warm hands, wondering why anyone ever thought bravery had anything to do with riding Alpine passes in mid-October. The other quiet hero was the BMW Motorrad ConnectedRide Navigator, the GPS unit above the dash, which I came to treat as a third member of the expedition. It is controlled by the rotary dial just ahead of the left grip, so I never had to take a glove off or a hand off the bars. I had loaded the daily routes I’d planned at home. Twelve GPX files, one for each day, went in through the BMW Motorrad Connected app, and every morning, the unit simply knew where we were going. Better still, it let me tell the motorcycle what kind of road I wanted: very twisty, moderately twisty or sensibly straight. I could ask it to avoid motorways and toll roads altogether. Where an ordinary satnav would have hustled us down the fastest road, this one, with a little encouragement from my thumb, kept finding the road worth riding. Over twelve days, it took us on a string of roads I would never have found on my own. That was how we found the road to Passo Falzarego and a procession of bends I’d happily call unreasonable, in the best way. Auntie Claude had warned me of the possibility of closed passes and snow. The passes, evidently, had not got her memo. Falzarego led to Passo Giau, which, as many riders will agree, is the most beautiful pass in the Dolomites. The road climbs through hairpin after hairpin into a wide, bare bowl ringed by rock, and the GS went up it as if it had been waiting all week for the invitation. Part of the secret is the boxer’s low, wide cylinders, which pull the centre of gravity down, so a motorcycle this heavy turns in like something much lighter. I braked late, leaned into corners at angles that would make Newton neurotic and got back on the throttle early, delighted by the feel of the front wheel lifting. We stopped at the top for coffee and cake, the two BMWs parked in the sun and preening. From there, we descended through Val di Zoldo, stopping at Rifugio San Sebastiano for a hearty salami and cheese sandwich and indulgent hot chocolate on Passo Duran, then continued to Venas di Cadore. We were meant to stay the night in the town of San Vito di Cadore, but our booking was cancelled because my credit card payment hadn’t gone through. It turned out to be the best thing my card did all year. A last-minute scramble found us a room at Dolomiti Lodge Villa Gaia, in a village ten kilometres away, and it became the best stay of the trip. We walked in expecting a bed and a plate of pasta. We walked out feeling like regulars at a village wedding. Dinner that evening at the lodge’s restaurant felt like one long communal table. Everyone talked to everyone, even to us, though we knew no Italian, rounds of drinks were bought for us, and people drifted over to say hello. Most of the diners were locals who knew the staff, but nobody treated us as outsiders. The staff came from Albania, Italy, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and they worked the room like a well-rehearsed dance. Music played, feet skipped between tables, and now and then a waitress broke into a small pirouette on her way to the kitchen. It was joyful, noisy and entirely unpretentious. The food kept pace. I opted for the wild pigeon, a bird I was trying for the first time. Where I come from, pigeons are treated as a civic nuisance, so there was a certain poetic justice in the exercise. It was really very good. Villa Gaia was the southernmost point and the happiest evening of our trip, and without anyone saying so, it became the hinge. From there, every road pointed north and back towards Munich. We still rode some glorious ones: from Cortina into East Tyrol, a night at Bergmanns Ferienapartment in Debant, a day on the Grossglockner High Alpine Road in Austria, then Kitzbühel and St. Johann in Tirol. The colours stayed blazing, the roads stayed dry, and the GS kept doling out delight. But the mood of the trip had undergone a subtle change. The days that had begun with a hunger to reach the next pass now began with the gentle awareness that this was the home run, and that real life, with its emails and credit card bills, was waiting somewhere beyond the Bavarian border. It is an odd feeling, fully enjoying something and mourning it at the same time. And then we rolled back into Munich, and I hauled the BMW R 1300 GS onto the main stand for the final time. Twelve days earlier, I had been apprehensive about handling this big motorcycle. Now I unloaded my luggage with the sort of reluctance people usually reserve for goodbyes at airports. I gave the tank one last pat, fondly, and walked away. The Key Monastery blends into Spiti’s spectacular landscape. title: GS Law mobilizes 2nd regional leg of West PH Sea Maritime Security Forum in Tarlac - University of Santo Tomas
content: The UST Graduate School of Law, in collaboration with the Tarlac State University School of Law, concluded the 2nd Regional leg of the West Philippine Sea Arbitral Ruling Forum on November 6, 2026, at the Old SP Session Hall, Capitol Building in Tarlac. The title of the second forum was “Upholding Sovereignty Through Law: Diplomacy, United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and the Rationale of the 2016 Arbitral Award.” Former Supreme Court Associate Justice Hon. Francis H. Jardeleza and Atty. Jewel Dela Cruz shared their expertise as speakers, with Atty. Carisa Balilia providing thoughtful insights as a reactor. The lecture gave enriching perspectives on the legal, diplomatic, and historical foundations of the Philippines’ maritime rights in the contested sea. The initiative aimed to mobilize Filipino voices and entrusted the potential second case against China to the youth. Jardeleza served as the Solicitor General (2012–2014) and led the Philippine legal team in the landmark UNCLOS maritime arbitration against China. The first Regional Leg of the forum, titled “Batangas Securing the Maritime Frontier: Strategic Defense,” was held last Oct. 23, 2026, in collaboration with the University of Batangas College of Law. Anchored on the overall theme “Upholding Sovereignty Through Law: Diplomacy, UNCLOS, and the Rationale of the 2016 Arbitral Award,” the program brought together an engaged audience of law students, fisherfolk, TSU officials, the Armed Forces of the Philippines, legal practitioners, and advocates for an insightful and meaningful discussion. The third and last leg, titled “People at the Frontline: Building Resilient Coastal Communities amid West Philippine Sea Tensions”, will be staged at the Palawan State University on January 29, 2027. With support from the Public Diplomacy Section of the U.S. Embassy in Manila, the caravan kicked off at the UST on Sept. 25. 2026. It was spearheaded by GS Law and the Faculty of Civil Law, together with the UST Research and Endowment Foundation, Inc. title: 2027 Federal Pay Raise: Up to 6.7% for Some as OPM Expands Special Rates - www.myfederalretirement.com

Financial Planning Resources for Federal & Postal Employees Most civilian federal employees are headed for a 0% raise in January 2027, but the plan for law enforcement runs in the opposite direction. A Nov. 6 memo from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) says employees already on the law enforcement special rate tables will receive 3.8%, while employees newly brought under those tables will receive about 6.7%, subject to pay caps and agency review. The memo implements a directive in the president’s Aug. 26 alternative pay plan, which freezes General Schedule (GS) base and locality pay at 2026 levels while ordering a 3.8% increase for covered law enforcement personnel through special pay authorities. The memo is CPM 2026-13, signed by Veronica E. Hinton, Associate Director for Workforce Policy and Innovation, and addressed to agency chief human capital officers. Its title says “Request for Information,” but agencies only need to respond in two cases: to opt out of the new coverage, or to send questions or comments. Both are due Nov. 25, 2026. OPM organizes the law enforcement special rates into three groups of tables. Where an employee lands determines the increase. In January 2026, everyone received a 1% base pay increase. Employees on Tables L001 through L140 also received a 2.77% special rate increase, which brought their total to 3.8% (1.038 ÷ 1.01 − 1). Employees brought under the special rates in 2027 never received that 2.77%. Open Season is your chance to review your coverage before another year of premiums and out-of-pocket expenses. This FREE November 17 webinar breaks down 2027 plan changes, employee costs, government contributions, and FSA options. Save your seat today! OPM says the goal is common pay levels for covered law enforcement positions. Newly covered employees therefore get the 2.77% on top of the 3.8%, which compounds to 6.68% (1.038 × 1.0277 − 1). For GS employees, the memo lists four categories to be extended coverage: OPM says it plans to extend 6.68% to some non-GS positions as well: FP-1811 criminal investigators at the Department of Commerce and the Peace Corps, and non-supervisory SK-1811 criminal investigators at the Securities and Exchange Commission, the latter subject to consultation with OPM. Non-GS positions that received 3.8% in 2026 stay at 3.8%: the Secret Service Uniformed Division, Diplomatic Security Service agents and criminal investigators, U.S. Park Police, and National Nuclear Security Administration nuclear materials couriers. Separately, OPM is considering 3.8% special rates for Customs and Border Protection agricultural inspectors and certain firefighters. The memo describes these as protective positions rather than law enforcement occupations, and OPM staff will contact agencies for staffing data. Special rates cannot exceed level IV of the Executive Schedule, which stays at $197,200 in 2027 under the alternative pay plan. A second limit says the minimum rate of a special rate schedule for a grade cannot be more than 30% above the maximum basic pay otherwise payable for that grade, excluding locality pay. The memo warns that employees at or near either limit may see no increase, or less than 3.8% (current) or 6.7% (newly covered). For salary context, see the GS pay scale page. OPM says special rates are basic pay for most purposes, including retirement. The raise therefore feeds the High-3 average salary used to calculate a Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) pension, not only take-home pay. The first illustration uses the basic FERS formula of 1% of High-3 for each year of service, with 30 years of service and a $90,000 High-3: Employees covered by the FERS special retirement provisions for law enforcement officers use a higher formula: 1.7% of High-3 for each of the first 20 years of service and 1% for each year after that. Coverage under those provisions is a separate question from special rate coverage, and the definitions differ, so check the position’s retirement coverage on OPM’s FERS computation page. For an employee with 25 years of service, the multiplier is 39%: Both illustrations assume the raise applies to the full 36-month High-3 window. For an employee retiring in 2027 or 2028, only part of the window includes the higher pay, so the effect is smaller at first and builds as more months at the new rate enter the average. The memo does not create a governmentwide raise. Under the alternative pay plan, most GS employees remain at 0% in January unless Congress acts. Retiree cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) follow a separate statutory formula, and the 2027 figures are tracked on the COLA Watch page. title: Karol G’s concert takes a terrifying turn as cameraman falls in front of stunned fans - MARCA
content: Karol G’s concert takes a terrifying turn as cameraman falls in front of stunned fans The accident occurred during the singer's second performance in Monterrey, when one of the devices used to record the show got caught on the worker's backpack and lifted him several meters before causing him to fall. Karol G's concert in Monterrey had an episode no one expected. While the Colombian singer was performing her second show at Estadio BBVA, one of the cameramen on her production team ended up suspended in the air after getting snagged by a drone. The moment was recorded by several attendees and quickly began circulating on social media. The images show how the worker is suddenly lifted up and, seconds later, falls next to the stage. The accident caused concern among the spectators, who began asking what had happened and, above all, how the young man was doing. The incident occurred on Saturday November 7, 2026, during Karol G's second performance in Monterrey. At that moment, the artist was performing her song "Te llevas to" when an aerial camera apparently got caught on the backpack worn by one of the technical crew members. The force of the device lifted him several meters above the stage. However, the harness ended up coming loose and the cameraman fell into the space between the main structure and the seating area. Production staff rushed to help him after the accident. Another detail that drew attention was the singer's reaction. According to the footage released, Karol G had her back turned to the area where the accident occurred, so she apparently did not notice what was happening and continued performing the song. The show continued without interruptions, while attendees watched what had happened and shared the recordings on social media. The cameraman's health condition  is one of the main unknowns left by the accident. As of November 9, no official information had been released about the worker's identity, the possible injuries he suffered, or whether he needed medical attention after the fall. Although some social media posts began to mention possible fractures, that information has not been confirmed by the production team or by official sources. For now, the video of the accident is the main public record of what happened. © 2026  Unidad Editorial Información Deportiva, S.L.U. All rights reserved. title: Bengaluru to host first standalone Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians' conference on November 17-18 - The New Indian Express
content: BENGALURU: Bengaluru will host the first standalone Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians (CWP) India Region Conference in the country on November 17 and 18, bringing together around 150 women legislators from across India and representatives from 15-20 countries to deliberate on women's political leadership, cyber safety and capacity building. Announcing the event at a press conference at Vidhana Soudha on Monday, Karnataka Legislative Assembly Speaker G S Patil and Legislative Council Chairman Saleem Ahmed said the two-day event would provide a platform for women parliamentarians and legislators to discuss the challenges they face in public life and explore ways to strengthen their participation in legislative and decision-making processes. "This is a matter of pride for Karnataka. It is the first time that a standalone Commonwealth Women Parliamentarians conference of this nature is being organised in India, and Bengaluru has been chosen to host it," Patil said. The conference will be inaugurated by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Chief Minister D K Shivakumar. Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman Harivansh, Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara and CWP India Region Chairperson D Purandeswari will also participate in the inaugural session. Around 150 delegates, including women MPs, MLAs, Members of Legislative Councils, Speakers and Deputy Speakers from various States and Union Territories, are expected to attend. Four women legislators from each State are expected to be represented. Representatives from 15-20 countries are also likely to participate. The conference will focus on two major themes — women's safety in the digital and cyberspace environment and strengthening the legislative skills and leadership capabilities of women representatives. The deliberations will cover cybercrimes against women, online harassment, digital abuse, misuse of artificial intelligence, deepfake technology, and protection of personal information and digital privacy. The discussions will also examine the challenges faced by women elected representatives in the digital environment. The second theme will focus on capacity building, including legislative procedures, lawmaking, policymaking, parliamentary debates, leadership development and the effective use of technology in legislative functioning. "Women's representation in legislative institutions is important, but it is equally necessary to strengthen their capabilities and ensure that they have a meaningful role in policymaking and governance. The conference will provide an opportunity to discuss the challenges faced by women legislators and share experiences," Saleem Ahmed said. He said the Karnataka Legislature had been asked to host the conference and the detailed agenda was being worked out in consultation with the Lok Sabha Secretariat and the CWP leadership. Purandeswari has constituted a committee of around 27-28 MPs, which has already held preliminary meetings in connection with the conference preparations, he said. The event will begin with the inaugural session at 11 am on November 17, at Banquet Hall in Vidhana Soudha, followed by deliberations after lunch. The valedictory session will be held at noon on November 18, with Governor Sudha Yadav participating. A curtain-raiser programme will be organised on November 14, with Chief Minister D K Shivakumar and CWP India Region Chairperson D Purandeswari unveiling the conference poster and outlining the preparations. Patil said Karnataka had accorded prominence to women's participation in public life and the conference would send a strong message on women's empowerment across the country. When asked about the absence of women in the State Cabinet, Patil said there were two  vacancies at present and women would be accommodated. As part of the conference-related programme, delegates will also be taken on a visit to Mysuru on November 19, including to Chamundi Hills. The conference is expected to provide a national and international platform to discuss ways of making legislative institutions more inclusive and strengthening women's leadership in democratic governance. title: [Exclusive] “Let’s capture the 2,800-trillion AI infrastructure market” ... POSCO, GS forge data center “alliance” - 매일경제
content:
POSCO and GS are joining forces to target the artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) market. They will combine POSCO’s steel materials and solutions with GS Group’s overseas sales and construction capabilities. Together, they aim to target the global data center market. According to industry sources on the 9th, POSCO and GS are pursuing business cooperation related to AIDCs. The partnership is expected to be formalized within this month. Although concerns about regulations on data center construction have grown since the recent U.S. midterm elections, the plan is to use the cooperation to strengthen each company’s business competitiveness and open up new markets to overcome sluggishness in existing demand industries. McKinsey & Company estimates that, of the investment needed to build AI data centers worldwide from 2025 to 2030, construction and development—including land, materials and site development—will amount to $800 billion (about 1,080 trillion won), while infrastructure—including power generation, transmission and cooling—will total $1.3 trillion (about 1,755 trillion won). This is a market that POSCO and GS, with their materials and energy supply capabilities, could seek to enter. Although the specific scope of the businesses and the projects involved have yet to be determined, areas of cooperation under consideration include supplying specialized steel products needed for data centers and power infrastructure, and identifying overseas projects, based on the companies’ existing businesses. POSCO established its Future Demand Development Office last July as part of its effort to become a specialized steelmaker covering AI- and power-related materials and solutions. The office serves as a control tower, moving beyond market responses organized by individual products to coordinate POSCO’s full range of products in response to demand across growth industries. Last month, POSCO separately formed an AIDC Demand Development Project Team and an ESS Specialized Solutions Project Team, and established a collaboration framework with affiliates including POSCO International, POSCO E&C and POSCO A&C. POSCO offers a range of materials and solutions, from structural steel for buildings to cold-rolled steel sheets for server racks, highly corrosion-resistant PosMAC, stainless steel for cooling pipes and electrical steel for transformers. It recently also developed an electromagnetic shielding steel sheet, “PosMAC Shield,” combining electrical steel and galvanized steel. Within GS Group, GS Global Corp., GS Engineering & Construction and GS Caltex are central to a range of capabilities related to data center construction, from connecting overseas supply chains to construction, cooling and power. GS Global Corp. opened a branch in Houston, U.S., last August and expanded its local sales network alongside its existing Los Angeles entity. It has built a network connecting local engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) firms with steel processors and distributors, and plans to step up support for winning orders and identifying new businesses starting next year. Drawing on experience with projects such as the Anyang Epoch Data Center, GS Engineering & Construction is building a business model that links investment, development, construction and operations. GS Caltex has strengthened its competitiveness in cooling technology by launching a dedicated cooling fluid to remove heat from data center servers.
